podcasts.name: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Acknowledged Dylan's Talent
podcast.body: Despite the initial bitterness some felt towards Dylan's ambition, Van Ronk remained friendly and acknowledged Dylan's talent, secure in his own abilities. "Van Runk, who did more for Dylan than anyone else on the scene, never really was."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Live Act Highlight
podcast.body: Dave Van Ronk's arrangement of "House of the Rising Sun" quickly became the most requested song and the highlight of his live performances. "House of the Rising Sun soon became the highlight of Van Runk's live act and his most requested song."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 115: "House of the Rising Sun" by the Animals

podcast.title: Mentor to Bob Dylan
podcast.body: Van Ronk was a crucial mentor to Bob Dylan for about six months. Dylan consciously sought him out to imitate, often slept on his couch, and was briefly managed by Van Ronk's wife. Van Ronk provided many arrangements that Dylan copied for his debut album. "Van Runk was an important mentor to him for a crucial period of six months or so"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Most Important Blues and Ballad Folk Musician
podcast.body: Dave Van Ronk was considered the most important musician within the blues and ballads group of folkies in Greenwich Village. "Van Runk was the most important musician in the blues and ballads group of folkies"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Musical Background
podcast.body: A physically large man, he started as a traditional jazz guitarist and banjo player before transitioning to folk music due to his love for blues singers like Bessie Smith and folk blues artists like Lead Belly. "A physically massive man, he'd started out as a traditional jazz guitarist and banjo player, but had slowly moved on into the folk side of things, through his love of blues singers like Bessie Smith and folk blues artists like Lead Belly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Native New Yorker
podcast.body: He was one of the few native New Yorkers in the Greenwich Village scene, hailing from Queens. "Van Runk was one of the few people on the village scene who was a native New Yorker, though he was from Queens rather than the village"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: New Orleans Prison Theory
podcast.body: Van Ronk initially believed "House of the Rising Sun" was about a brothel, but later speculated it was actually about the New Orleans women's prison, which he believed bore a carving of a rising sun over its doorway. "Van Runk, who put the song into the form by which it became best known, believed at first that it was a song about a brothel, but he later decided it was probably about the new Orleans women's prison, which in his accounting used to have a carving of a rising sun over the doorway."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 115: "House of the Rising Sun" by the Animals

podcast.title: Origin of Arrangement
podcast.body: Dave Van Ronk's influential arrangement of "House of the Rising Sun" originated from a 1938 field recording by Alan Lomax of George Eterner from Kentucky, which Van Ronk learned from a 1953 record by Halley Wood. "Van Runk's version traces back originally to a field recording Alan Lohmach's had made in 1938 of a woman named George Eterner from Kent Tucket."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 115: "House of the Rising Sun" by the Animals

podcast.title: Political Stance
podcast.body: Van Ronk was an anarchist who, through his association with the Shaktimanites (a fringe left group with Trotskyite and anarchist leanings), began to convert to Marxism. "politically anarchist who, through his connection with the Shaktimanites, a fringe left group who were more trotsghett than the trotsghett, and whose views sometimes shaded in to anarchism was becoming converted to Marxism."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Stopped Performing Live
podcast.body: Van Ronk eventually ceased performing "House of the Rising Sun" live because he grew tired of people mistakenly identifying it as "that Dylan song." "Van Runk did record his version, as we heard, but he soon stopped playing the song live, because he got sick of people telling him to play that Dylan song."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 115: "House of the Rising Sun" by the Animals

podcast.title: Student of Reverend Gary Davis
podcast.body: Van Ronk studied the technique of Reverend Gary Davis, a blind gospel blues singer, learning a great deal from him. "Van Runk had learned a great deal from Reverend Gary Davis, a blind gospel blues singer whose technique Van Runk had studied."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Unimpressed by Robert Johnson's Originality
podcast.body: When Bob Dylan played Robert Johnson's "King of the Delta Blues Singers" for him, Van Ronk was unimpressed by Johnson's musical originality, demonstrating to Dylan how Johnson had borrowed ideas from other artists like Skip James and Lee Roy Carr. "Musically, Johnson just didn't seem very original to Van Rung, who played Dylan records by Skip James, Lee Roy Car and others, showing Dylan where Johnson had picked up most of his musical ideas."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
